inventory.scope: Selected scientific construction, caption/figure interpretation and custody clauses in 23 assigned liquid-biopsy support paths, with all eligible associated context. Not a replacement ordinary-lesson denominator.

rows.requirement: The count model concerns original target molecules in one evaluated aliquot of a fixed volume, before workflow recovery and calling.
Independent random Poisson inclusion is an explicit fictional assumption, not an empirically validated ctDNA sampling law in every specimen.
For that count model, P(N=0)=exp(-lambda), with lambda the expected count; lambda zero is the degenerate zero-count case.
At lambda one the zero-count probability is exp(-1)=0.36787944117144233, displayed as 36.8 percent or about 37 percent.
The 201 curve points and seven anchors cover lambda zero through five and must match the declared model, rather than clinical observations.
The 0/1/2 aliquot drawings illustrate possible counts, not observed frequencies or equal probabilities.
More reads cannot recover an original molecule that was absent from the evaluated aliquot; amplification does not create independent starting molecules.
Sampling absence, workflow loss, detector/calling failure and biological cancer absence are separate possibilities.
The 36.8-percent toy result is not a clinical false-negative rate, LoD, negative predictive value or individual probability of cancer.
The figure supplies neither a clinical sample volume nor a timeline; repeated draws are not assumed independent.
ctDNA is the tumor-derived part of recovered cfDNA; the broader extracellular-DNA pool can have tumor and non-tumor sources.
Defined source classes differ from assignment of an unknown sampled fragment; known non-tumor class lies outside the tumor-derived subset by definition.
Both dashed routes in the separate unknown-fragment task remain unselected, so the observed fragment is not assigned to either source.
Recovered total DNA yield is an amount measurement and alone does not identify tumor origin or tumor fraction.
Equal fictional one-milliliter aliquots yielding two and four nanograms show doubled total yield without measuring tumor-attributed change.
A real plasma sequence can have blood-cell rather than solid-tumor origin; measurement accuracy and source attribution are distinct.
A shared blood-cell variant supports a blood-cell contribution without making every possible tumor contribution impossible.
Reference comparisons and origin filters retain coverage, sensitivity, timing and specimen-representativeness limits.
Fragments and schematic source areas do not count living cells, identify lesions or establish treatment utility.
The two invented plasma aliquots each have one milliliter volume and four tumor-attributed molecule symbols.
Aliquot A has sixteen background molecules and twenty total; aliquot B has thirty-six background and forty total.
Both toy concentrations remain four tumor-attributed molecules per milliliter.
The recovered-molecule shares are 4/20=20 percent and 4/40=10 percent; the share halves without a change in tumor-attributed amount per volume.
A recovered-molecule share is not automatically a variant allele fraction, model-estimated tumor fraction or MTM/mL output.
Concentration requires a volume denominator and fraction requires the named evaluated pool; assay recovery and calibration constrain conversions.
PPM is a rescaling of the same specified fraction, not a change of measured quantity.
A 0.01-percent variant allele fraction equals one hundred PPM of evaluated variant-supporting alleles, not automatically one hundred PPM tumor fraction.
Detection and reliable quantitation need their separate input-dependent validated conditions; a printed value alone does not establish a precise fold change.
The illustration depicts one marker-dependent cell-enrichment workflow followed by separate cell-identification rules.
Recovered qualifying cells, unselected cells and extracellular DNA fragments are separate entities or outputs.
Surface-marker enrichment can miss cells with inadequate marker expression; marker-independent selection also has method-specific recovery bias.
The historical epithelial-cell example uses EpCAM enrichment with nuclear, cytokeratin and CD45-negative classification under its own device rules.
Icons are fictional and not measured prevalence or universal recovery proportions.
Zero qualifying cells in a finite 7.5-milliliter sample does not establish zero circulating tumor cells in the body.
Free DNA fragments are outside the recovered-cell count because they are a distinct analyte, so the CTC result does not dictate a ctDNA result.
Recovery and classification do not establish a cell's viability, metastatic capability, lesion of origin or genomic profile.
A prognostic CTC association is separate from evidence that a count-triggered treatment change improves outcomes.
Fragment length, ends, genomic positions and chemical marks are measured features used before model-based source inference.
Schematic colors and dots distinguish drawing objects or marks, not known malignant identities or cancer addresses.
Normal cell types also carry methylation patterns, and a mixture can contain normal and tumor contributors.
Reference-atlas deconvolution and classifier scores are method-dependent inferences rather than direct cell counts.
A normal-organ contribution can change with tissue injury; inferred organ source alone does not prove cancer.
Collection and processing can alter source mixture and recovered features, even if overall DNA yield is adequate.
Missing reference cell types, handling changes and population shifts can affect interpretation under a fixed model.
A model score need not be a calibrated probability and does not by itself establish diagnosis, site, stage or treatment benefit.
The fictional changed-transport example does not prove more cancer-associated DNA when only a model score rises.
The blood-cell clone and solid-tumor compartments are parallel possible contributors to plasma DNA.
The generic variant V is detected in fictional plasma and blood-cell DNA but not detected in the sampled tumor material.
The blood match supports a blood-cell contribution; tumor non-detection remains bounded by sampled region, timing, coverage and sensitivity.
A shared mutation and an ambiguous-source category prevent simple subtraction from being a perfect origin filter.
Blood-cell origin is different from sequencing error, formal CHIP classification and a clinical-risk forecast.
A clone below a conventional CHIP threshold can still contribute a real plasma variant; variant allele fraction is not automatically cell percentage.
The sample comparison is constructed teaching data and supplies neither empirical source proportions nor a universal cutoff.
All six fictional cases recur at month twelve and have scheduled blood draws every two months from zero through twelve.
A-D have first qualifying positives at months ten, eight, six and four, giving gaps of two, four, six and eight months.
The selected median is (4+6)/2=five months among the four completed earlier-positive intervals.
E and F have no earlier qualifying positive and are excluded from that median rather than silently assigned zero-month lead time.
The observed earlier-positive date does not locate biological onset because sampling and clinical ascertainment are intermittent.
Lead-time interpretation requires event definitions, collection/reporting/confirmation dates, schedules and the evaluated denominator.
A selected timing median establishes neither improved survival nor intervention benefit or a personal future interval.
Follow-up without a completed recurrence interval and missed detections require separate handling rather than zero or infinite lead time.
Unrelated studies' lead-time medians do not establish an assay-performance ranking.
The comparison axis is the reference used to construct the detector, not an intrinsic sensitivity hierarchy.
A tumor-informed mutation strategy selects tracking features from suitable sampled tumor material; reference quality and representativeness constrain it.
A tumor-naive strategy begins with predefined features or rules without first building that person's tumor-derived detector.
Both routes meet a shared illustrative finite plasma-input stage; one drawn tube does not duplicate molecules or certify equal performance.
Source attribution, handling, recovery, qualifying-call rules and intended-use validation apply to both designs.
If fictional method A requires unavailable suitable tumor material, it cannot build its reference; that failure is not a negative plasma result.
Fictional predefined method B can start with qualifying plasma under its own rules, without proving detection beyond its feature list.
A fixed tumor-tracking list cannot establish detection of variants absent from that list, and a predefined panel also has finite feature scope.
Different disease burdens, time points, cohorts, missing samples and outcome definitions preclude a universal winner from unrelated positivity percentages.
Detection ability alone does not establish benefit from acting on an assay result.
